what_it_does: Training very large AI models requires splitting the model's enormous weight matrices across dozens or hundreds of chips and doing a massive collective operation — called an 'all-reduce' — where every chip adds up contributions from every other chip after computing its local portion. When only one dimension of splitting is used (one-dimensional parallelism), the all-reduce traffic grows linearly with the number of chips, becoming a severe bottleneck at scale. MeshSlice introduces a new algorithm for performing large matrix multiplications (the core arithmetic operation in AI training) split across a two-dimensional grid of chips, where instead of one big all-reduce at the end, smaller partial communication steps are interleaved with ongoing arithmetic, so the chips are computing and communicating simultaneously rather than taking turns. An automatic tuner searches over how to shape the chip grid, how many slices to split the work into, and how to arrange the dataflow, to find the fastest configuration for each layer of the model and each cluster size.
